Lessons.Title: Build It
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Construct segments, lines and circles precisely with a straightedge and compass. Explain how equal compass openings justify equal distances.

Starting model (verbal diagram, not to scale): A and B are distinct points; a circle with centre A passes through B. Every point P on that circle satisfies AP = AB. A straightedge draws the unique line through two distinct marked points; a compass transfers a fixed distance without reading a ruler.

Construction is not tracing by eye. A justified line is defined by two distinct points, and a justified circle by its centre and a point/radius. For a reproducible paper construction, mark named points and keep the compass opening fixed when transferring lengths.

U01:L01 repair (2026-10-30), first-party activity A — compare a freehand sketch with tool-defined construction: given distinct points P,Q and a separate point A, use the compass opening PQ to draw a circle centred at A, choose B on that circle, draw a second circle centred at B through A, and join A to B. Explain which distances are guaranteed equal and why a hand-drawn imitation alone cannot guarantee them. On paper, use an unmarked straightedge and compass; a compatible digital tool is optional, not claimed integrated.

U01:L01 repair (2026-10-30), first-party activity B — diagnose an illegal move: J and K are distinct. A learner estimates a midpoint M on JK by eye, then asserts JM = MK and JK = 2JM. Neither equality is guaranteed. To replace the guess, draw congruent arcs centred at J and K with a common radius greater than JK/2; their two intersections define the perpendicular bisector and exact midpoint. The teacher reviews the actual labelled construction and argument, not a numeric proxy.

Source-exact exploratory sequence for 1.2 (original Edulytiks wording): start with distinct A,B. Draw the circle centred at A through B; ESTIMATE a point C halfway along AB, without measuring or proving it. Draw the circle centred at B through C, label its two intersections with the first circle D and E, and connect A-D-E. Compare the produced triangles across two students BEFORE checking whether C really bisects AB. Different C choices change BC, the second circle and D,E; even though AD = AE = AB, the shape is not necessarily reproducible. Only after this comparison demonstrate equal-radius arcs as a legitimate exact-midpoint construction.

U01:L01 repair (2026-10-30), first-party activity C — independently sketch a regular hexagon, then construct one by stepping a fixed compass radius as successive chords on a circle. Compare the two results and justify equal sides using radius-defined equilateral central triangles; six central angles of 60° complete 360°. A peer comparison, diagram and explanation are assessed by a teacher.

Original Edulytiks task: Given distinct points A and B, construct an equilateral triangle ABC using two equal-radius circles. Record each permitted compass and straightedge move and explain why all three sides have the same length.

Human assessment boundary: an actual learner drawing and tool use are evaluated with a teacher rubric; no generated numeric answer is evidence of a successful physical construction. Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 1 Lesson 1, CC BY 4.0; independently authored Edulytiks explanations and questions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Straightedge
KeyConcepts.Definition: A straightedge defines a straight line through two distinct points without measuring its length.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Mark A and B, then draw line AB or the finite segment AB using the points as anchors.
KeyConcepts.Example: For A ≠ B, segment AB includes endpoints A and B; ray AB starts at A and continues through B.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compass and circle
KeyConcepts.Definition: A circle is the set of points at a fixed positive distance r from a fixed centre O.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A compass centred at O and opened to OA draws the circle through A; the unchanged opening transfers OA.
KeyConcepts.Example: If P lies on this circle, OP = OA by construction.

KeyConcepts.Title: Construction evidence
KeyConcepts.Definition: A geometric construction is justified by tool actions and invariants, not by visual resemblance.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Name the constructed points and state equal-radius or collinearity reasons.
KeyConcepts.Example: If C lies on circles with centres A and B of radius AB, then AC = BC = AB.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two circles make an equilateral triangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Given distinct points A and B, construct C so that △ABC has three equal sides.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use circles with centres at A and B and the same nonzero radius AB.
Steps: Draw segment AB with the straightedge.
With centre A and opening AB draw circle cA.
Without changing the opening, draw circle cB centred at B.
Choose either intersection C of cA and cB and draw AC and BC.
Because C is on cA, AC = AB. Because C is on cB, BC = AB. Therefore AC = BC = AB.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Triangle ABC is equilateral; either circle intersection is a valid choice.
WorkedExamples.Check: A and B must be distinct. Two equal circles of radius AB intersect in two points, one on either side of AB. Teacher checks placement and marked equality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Transfer a length without reading a scale
WorkedExamples.Question: Given segment PQ and a distinct point R, how can you locate S with RS = PQ?
WorkedExamples.Method: Fix the compass opening to the distance PQ.
Steps: Place the compass point at P and pencil at Q to capture opening PQ.
Keep the opening unchanged and place the compass point at R.
Mark any point S on the resulting circle centred at R.
Draw segment RS with the straightedge and label its endpoints.
WorkedExamples.Answer: RS = PQ by equal compass radius.
WorkedExamples.Check: The direction of RS is not fixed by its length; many S points are valid.

WorkedExamples.Title: Six equal chords form a regular hexagon
WorkedExamples.Question: Construct a regular hexagon with a given circle centre O and radius OA > 0.
WorkedExamples.Method: Step a chord equal to the circle radius around the circle.
Steps: Draw the circle centred at O through A.
Keep the compass opening OA. From A mark the next point B on the circle.
Repeat at successive vertices to obtain C, D, E and F, then join consecutive points and F to A.
Each central triangle such as OAB has all sides radius OA and is equilateral, so each central angle is 60 degrees.
Six 60-degree central angles complete a full 360-degree turn; each chord has length OA.
WorkedExamples.Answer: ABCDEF is a regular hexagon with six equal sides and six equal central angles.
WorkedExamples.Check: Vertices must be taken consecutively in one direction. The compass opening remains OA throughout.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Eyeballing the location of a point that ought to be an exact circle intersection.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Visual estimates do not establish fixed distances and may break an equality claim.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use two defined circles and select a labelled intersection; justify equality using the radius definition.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Changing the compass opening between equal-radius circles.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The side lengths then need not be equal.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep the compass opening AB fixed for both circles in the triangle construction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Estimating the midpoint of a segment by eye and calling the resulting figure an exact construction.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Visual placement cannot guarantee equal half-segment lengths; the dependent circle radius and figure vary between students.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Construct the perpendicular bisector from intersecting equal-radius arcs and justify both endpoint distances before naming the midpoint.

SummaryPoints: A straightedge supplies collinearity and a compass supplies equal distances.
Source-aligned mathematical goal: precise construction and explanation, not mere drawing by appearance.
First-party constructions and justifications are described without copying publisher graphics; teacher reviews actual drawings, tool decisions and written explanations.

An estimated midpoint is deliberately useful as an exploratory illegal move: compare the different constructed triangles first, then critique unsupported half-length equalities and construct a true midpoint.
Paper compass/straightedge evidence with a labelled diagram and written proof can assess the source construction skill; it is not an online uploaded drawing or automatically scored result.

Lessons.Title: Constructing Patterns
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Follow and write unambiguous straightedge-and-compass instructions that another person can use to reproduce a geometric pattern.

Verbal diagram: A and B are distinct endpoints of a horizontal segment. Two congruent circles centred at A and B both pass through the other centre. Label the intersection above AB as C and the one below as D. A reader can now construct the same four labelled points without needing an image.

Original Edulytiks construction challenge: create a diamond-shaped pattern from the two intersections C and D. Describe every point, centre, radius, intersection and segment in order; a peer should be able to follow the directions without seeing your result.

Rubric (teacher scored, 0–4): one point each for non-degenerate starting points and correctly maintained radius; unambiguous centre/intersection labels; correctly drawn segments; and a mathematical explanation of the equal lengths. A drawing or peer reconstruction is the evidence; no numeric-only automatic grade.

Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 1 Lesson 2, CC BY 4.0. These are independently authored Edulytiks construction instructions, not copies of the original pattern artwork.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reproducible directions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Construction instructions uniquely specify allowed steps and named geometric objects up to explicitly permitted choices.
KeyConcepts.Rule: State the starting data, tools, centre, radius, intersection choice and connecting order.
KeyConcepts.Example: ‘Draw a circle centred at A through B’ is reproducible; ‘draw a circle on the left’ is ambiguous.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal-radius intersections
KeyConcepts.Definition: A point lying on two equal-radius circles has equal distances to their two centres.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If C lies on both circles centred A and B with radius AB then AC = BC = AB.
KeyConcepts.Example: C above AB and D below AB are the two equilateral-triangle apexes.

KeyConcepts.Title: Pattern verification
KeyConcepts.Definition: A second student's successful reproduction requires mathematically precise inputs and a checkable invariant.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare named equal lengths or known geometric properties rather than the appearance of a sketch.
KeyConcepts.Example: The four edges AC, CB, BD and DA all have the same length.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct a symmetric four-sided pattern
WorkedExamples.Question: Given a nonzero segment AB, create the quadrilateral A–C–B–D whose four sides are equal.
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct two congruent circles and connect their two intersections.
Steps: Draw and label distinct A and B with segment AB.
Draw a circle centred at A through B.
With unchanged compass opening AB, draw a circle centred at B through A.
Label the intersection on one side of AB C, and the other D.
Draw AC, CB, BD and DA in that order.
Each of C and D lies on both radius-AB circles, so AC = BC = BD = DA = AB.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Quadrilateral A–C–B–D has four equal sides and is a rhombus (with AB as one diagonal).
WorkedExamples.Check: The two intersections must be distinct, which holds because A ≠ B and the circles have equal radius AB.

WorkedExamples.Title: Diagnose ambiguous directions
WorkedExamples.Question: Why can't a classmate reliably follow ‘draw two circles, then connect the points’?
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify the missing geometric constraints and specify a reproducible replacement.
Steps: The instruction does not say where each circle is centred.
It also omits the radius or the segment controlling the compass opening.
It fails to identify which intersection points and which connections to use.
Replace it with explicit circles centred at A and B, both of radius AB, and named intersections C and D.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The original wording underdetermines the construction; the revised directions define checkable steps.
WorkedExamples.Check: A new person can reconstruct the figure using only the starting distinct points and the written directions.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove a pattern edge equality
WorkedExamples.Question: A pattern uses C as the upper intersection and D as the lower intersection of the two equal-radius circles. Is AC equal to BD?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the definition of circles and equal compass opening.
Steps: C lies on the circle centred A with radius AB, so AC = AB.
D lies on the circle centred B with radius AB, so BD = AB.
By transitivity AC = BD.
The argument is true irrespective of how the diagram is rotated.
WorkedExamples.Check: The statement uses labelled point membership and does not rely on measuring the picture.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using ‘left’ or ‘above’ without specifying a reference orientation or named line.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A diagram may be rotated or reflected by another student.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Specify which side of directed AB or allow either intersection where symmetry permits.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Asserting that sides are equal because the pattern looks symmetric.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A freehand sketch may resemble a rhombus even with unequal lengths.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State that each edge is a radius of one of the equal-radius circles.

SummaryPoints: Construction instructions must give labelled objects, circle centres, radii and permitted choices.
A reproducible pattern can be checked with distance invariants even after translation or rotation.
Peer reconstruction and written precision are human-assessed; no fabricated numerical correctness score.

Lessons.Title: Construction Techniques 1: Perpendicular Bisectors
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a nonzero segment and explain why its constructed points are equally distant from the endpoints.

Verbal diagram (not to scale): segment AB is horizontal; X lies above AB and Y below AB. X and Y are the two intersections of equal-radius circles centred at A and B. The line XY crosses AB at its midpoint M and is perpendicular to AB.

A perpendicular bisector is a line through the midpoint of a segment meeting it at a right angle. For endpoints A and B with A ≠ B, choose a compass radius r strictly greater than half the length AB, so the two equal circles have distinct intersections X and Y.

Why the construction works: AX = BX and AY = BY because X and Y lie on both equal-radius circles. The line of points equidistant from A and B is perpendicular to AB through its midpoint; in this lesson that locus is explored and used as a conjecture, with a full proof developed later in the course.

Teacher-scored original Edulytiks task: construct XY and label A, B, X, Y, M. Provide a written explanation for the equal distances and a drawing showing XY meeting AB at M. The rubric requires two intersecting equal-radius arcs, the line through X and Y, identified midpoint and right angle, and a valid radius-based equal-distance statement. A typed number alone cannot demonstrate these.

Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 1 Lesson 3, CC BY 4.0. This authored example and verbal diagram are Edulytiks originals; source sequence is acknowledged but publisher artwork is not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Perpendicular bisector
KeyConcepts.Definition: A line that passes through the midpoint of segment AB and meets AB at 90 degrees.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Construct it with equal-radius arcs from A and B intersecting at two points X and Y, then draw line XY.
KeyConcepts.Example: For A = (−3,0) and B = (3,0), the perpendicular bisector is x = 0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equidistant locus
KeyConcepts.Definition: The set of points P for which PA = PB, for two distinct fixed points A and B.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Equal circles centred at A and B locate two such points; their connecting line is the perpendicular bisector.
KeyConcepts.Example: If X is an intersection of two radius-5 circles centred at A and B then XA = XB = 5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Radius condition
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two equal circles of radius r centred distance d apart have two intersection points exactly when r > d/2.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use a compass opening greater than half the segment length; do not use zero or too small a radius.
KeyConcepts.Example: For AB = 6, radius 4 works; radius 3 gives one tangent point and cannot determine line XY.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct the perpendicular bisector
WorkedExamples.Question: Given a 6 cm segment AB, construct its perpendicular bisector using only a straightedge and compass.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use arcs of radius 4 cm (any radius strictly greater than 3 cm works) from both endpoints.
Steps: Mark the distinct endpoints A and B of segment AB.
Open the compass to any radius greater than AB/2, for instance 4 cm when AB = 6 cm.
With centres A and B, draw equal-radius arcs that intersect on both sides of AB.
Label the intersections X and Y, and draw the line through X and Y.
Mark M where XY meets AB. The equidistant-line property gives AM = MB = 3 cm and a right angle between XY and AB.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Line XY is the perpendicular bisector; its intersection M is the midpoint of AB.
WorkedExamples.Check: AX = BX and AY = BY by equal-radius construction. Teacher checks geometric line and perpendicularity rather than treating a single length as complete evidence.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find the locus in coordinates
WorkedExamples.Question: For A = (−3,0), B = (3,0), determine all points P = (x,y) such that PA = PB.
WorkedExamples.Method: Equate squared distances and simplify, without losing distance domain information.
Steps: PA² = (x+3)² + y² and PB² = (x−3)² + y².
Set (x+3)² + y² = (x−3)² + y².
Expand: x²+6x+9+y² = x²−6x+9+y².
Subtract common terms to obtain 12x = 0, so x = 0.
Every point (0,y) has equal squared distances to A and B, so x=0 is the full locus.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The vertical line x = 0, perpendicular to AB through (0,0).
WorkedExamples.Check: No extraneous solutions were introduced: squared Euclidean distances are nonnegative and equality of their squares implies equality of distances.

WorkedExamples.Title: Identify a failed radius choice
WorkedExamples.Question: Two circle centres are 10 cm apart. Can radius 4 cm produce two arc intersections?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare twice the circle radius to the distance between centres.
Steps: The circles have equal radii r = 4 cm and centre distance d = 10 cm.
Their radius lengths sum to 8 cm, less than 10 cm.
The circles cannot meet because a point belonging to both would require a path of total length at most 8 cm between the centres.
Choose any r > 5 cm instead to obtain two intersections.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No. Radius 4 cm gives no intersection; a radius strictly greater than 5 cm is required.
WorkedExamples.Check: At r = 5 cm the circles touch at only one point, so two distinct points are still unavailable.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using radius less than or equal to half the segment length to create two arc intersections.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: There are no intersections if r < AB/2 and only one if r = AB/2.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the same opening at both endpoints and choose r > AB/2.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling any line through the midpoint the perpendicular bisector.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The line must also meet the original segment at 90 degrees.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Justify both midpoint and perpendicularity; the equal-radius intersection method produces the correct line.

SummaryPoints: Equal-radius circles give points equally distant from both endpoints.
The line through two appropriate circle intersections is the perpendicular bisector, provided the starting endpoints differ.
Drawing, labelled justification and tool operation are reviewed with a teacher rubric rather than an invented auto-grade.
